tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SIGCOMM'17 paper (Langley et al., Google) reports randomized production A/B trials of QUIC users (QUICg) against a TLS/TCP control group (TCPg); the 8.0%/3.6% mean Search Latency and 18.0%/15.3% mean Rebuffer Rate reductions appear in the Introduction and in Tables 1-2 of Section 6. No public benchmark code, compiler, flags or CPU model, so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Mean Google Search latency reduced 8.0% for desktop users and 3.6% for mobile users; mean YouTube Video Rebuffer Rate reduced 18.0% for desktop and 15.3% for mobile, QUICg vs the TLS/TCP control group (Introduction, and Section 6 'QUIC Performance', Tables 1 and 2). The same Table 1 also gives a mean Video Latency reduction of 8.0% for desktop and 5.3% for mobile.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 898 stars (2026-09-26). README: powers Google's servers, Chromium, Envoy and other projects. The paper says QUIC carried over 30% of Google's egress traffic (about 7% of Internet traffic) in 2017.
corrections.caveats: The numbers are from the SIGCOMM 2017 paper 'The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment'. They were measured on Google's original gQUIC code, then in Chromium (paper Section 3.9) and the ancestor of today's IETF-QUIC QUICHE, in live randomized production trials rather than a lab benchmark. The paper is first-party: all authors are at Google. The gains come mainly from protocol design (0-RTT handshakes, loss recovery), not from implementation speed. The paper also reports costs: QUIC server CPU was about 3.5x TLS/TCP at first and about 2x after optimization (Section 6.7), and QUIC can do worse than TCP on high-bandwidth (>100 Mbps) or very-low-RTT links (Section 6.8). No comparison is made against Cloudflare's Rust quiche, msquic, nghttp3 or c-ares. Google's C++ QUICHE is unrelated to Cloudflare's Rust 'quiche', despite the similar name. Standalone embedding needs platform API implementations; the README points to Chromium and Envoy for these.

notes: The PDF is live, and every claimed number matches the paper exactly. The only fix to claimed_speedup is the section reference: the paper has no 'Application Performance' section, and the figures sit in Section 6 'QUIC Performance'. The GitHub REST API was rate-limited (403), so the metadata came from other sources: license BSD-3-Clause from the raw LICENSE file and the repo page; not archived, not a fork, and 898 stars from the repo page HTML; last commit 2026-09-25 from the commits atom feed, so the repo is active.
